Part II:

I remember the exact moment vibe coding clicked for me. It was late at night, I was tinkering on a web app idea, and instead of manually writing functions, I found myself chatting with an AI assistant: “Add a login button here, make it blue and slightly bigger.” The code updated instantly. No stack overflow searches, no hunting down CSS files – just me and the AI, riffing in plain English. That’s when I realized: I had fully given in to the vibes .

In Part 1 of this article, I introduced the concept of vibe coding . Now, in Part 2, I’ll dive deeper into this emerging industry – from what exactly vibe coding means, to who’s riding this wave, what they’re building, and how it’s changing the craft of software development. This exploration is personal, told from my first-hand perspective as a developer-turned-vibe-coder navigating this brave new world.

slides.headline: What Does “Vibe Coding” Mean?
slides.body:
Let’s start with a definition. Vibe coding is a term coined in early 2025 by AI luminary Andrej Karpathy ​​. He described it as a new way to write software: you “fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists.” In practice, vibe coding means using conversational natural language prompts to guide large language model (LLM) coding assistants, rather than writing every line yourself.

When Karpathy first talked about it, he painted a vivid picture. He would speak to an AI-powered code editor (using voice commands, no less) and ask for “the dumbest things” like “decrease the padding on the sidebar by half” – tasks he used to do manually but now was too lazy to hunt for in code​. The AI (in his case, an IDE called Cursor paired with a model nicknamed “Sonnet”) would oblige, generating and modifying code on the fly. He’d hit “Accept All” on the changes without even reading the diffs. If a bug popped up or an error message appeared, he’d just paste it back to the AI and say, “Hey, fix this.” More often than not, the AI fixed it or at least tried alternative solutions.

slides.headline: ““I’m building a project or web app, but it’s not really coding – I just see stuff, say
slides.body:
““I’m building a project or web app, but it’s not really coding – I just see stuff, say stuff, run stuff, and copy-paste stuff, and it mostly works,” Karpathy admitted​ simonwillison.net .”

That, in essence, is vibe coding: treating coding like a conversation . You tell the computer what you want in plain language (the “vibe”), and the AI figures out the how . You don’t sweat the small stuff or obsess over each semicolon. You ride the wave of the AI’s exponential improvements in code generation. It’s coding, Jim, but not as we know it.

Crucially, vibe coding isn’t just using AI to assist coding – it’s a mindset of almost completely trusting the AI to write the code, while you guide and prod it along. In traditional coding, we write and then maybe get AI suggestions; in vibe coding, the AI writes and we suggest . It flips the script.

slides.headline: Who’s Riding the Vibe?
slides.body:
At first, vibe coding felt like a niche trick – a fun experiment for AI enthusiasts. But over the past months, it’s exploded into a whole movement. I’ve seen a wide spectrum of people embrace this style:

Hobbyists and Beginners: Perhaps the most excited group is non-coders and newcomers. Folks who once found programming intimidating are now dabbling with building apps by simply describing what they want. It still sounds like sci-fi: “Build me a simple game where a cat chases a laser pointer.” But I’ve watched with my own eyes as an AI actually generates the game code, assets and all, based on that request​ community.aws . One friend of mine who has zero coding background used a vibe coding tool to create a custom to-do list app for her phone – something she never dreamed she could do on her own. For her, and many like her, vibe coding is an entry point into software creation. They don’t call it “programming”; to them, it feels more like making a wish and having a genie (the AI) grant it . It’s incredibly empowering.

slides.headline: Indie Developers and Solo Makers: As an indie dev myself, I find vibe coding to be a
slides.body: Indie Developers and Solo Makers: As an indie dev myself, I find vibe coding to be a superpower for solo projects. It’s like having a junior programmer pair-programming with me, except this junior works at lightning speed and never sleeps. Indie game developers, for example, are vibing with AI to spin up game prototypes in days. I spoke with an acquaintance who built a text-based adventure game end-to-end by chatting with GPT-4 – designing levels, writing gameplay logic, fixing bugs, all via prompts. He said it felt more like playing than working. Likewise, indie web developers are using vibe coding to crank out SaaS app Minimum Viable Products on weekends. There’s an entire subculture on Twitter (or “X” as we call it now) and YouTube of these indie vibe-coders sharing screen recordings of themselves building apps from scratch just by describing features. It’s development as performance art.

slides.headline: Startups: In true Silicon Valley fashion, startups have jumped on vibe coding as the next
slides.body: Startups: In true Silicon Valley fashion, startups have jumped on vibe coding as the next competitive edge. Why hire 100 engineers when 10 can do the job with AI help? This isn’t just hypothetical – Y Combinator recently revealed that about a quarter of the startups in its Winter 2025 batch have codebases that are 95% AI-generated ​​. Think about that: these are real companies (with real money on the line) where almost all the code was produced by an AI. The founders are talented programmers in their own right, but they chose to “give in to the vibes” because it let them build product features ridiculously fast. I watched a YC roundtable video where the partners literally titled it “Vibe Coding Is the Future.” They discussed how even highly technical founders are leaning on AI to crank out code, allowing tiny teams to achieve what would have taken a large team much longer​. Startups are treating AI as a force multiplier – one founder described his AI pair-programmer as if he’d hired a hundred eager interns that never get tired.

slides.headline: Enterprises and Big Tech Teams: It’s not just the little guys.
slides.body: Enterprises and Big Tech Teams: It’s not just the little guys. Big companies are also experimenting (albeit more cautiously) with vibe coding techniques. For instance, Amazon has introduced an AI coding assistant called Amazon CodeWhisperer Q (or “Amazon Q Developer”), which integrates into their tooling. I tried out Amazon’s Q CLI tool in my own AWS projects – it lets me type natural language commands like “Set up a new Lambda function to process image uploads” , and it generates the scaffold code and configuration for me. It’s very much in the vibe coding spirit. Microsoft and Google are integrating similar AI copilots into their developer suites. Even historically conservative enterprise dev teams now have AI assistants embedded in IDEs or chat interfaces. I’ve heard of bank IT departments using internal GPT-based bots to generate boilerplate code for compliance reports, and of a major e-commerce company that built an internal “AI feature factory” where product managers can literally describe a feature and get a prototype web page generated. Enterprises see the productivity boost – one Fortune 500 CTO told me his dev team’s output has doubled since they started integrating AI into the development workflow. Of course, larger organizations are also more wary about code quality, security, and intellectual property, so they are keeping humans firmly in the loop (more on those concerns later). But the key point is: from basement startups to tech giants, everyone is testing the vibe .

slides.headline: Building on Vibes: What People Are Creating
slides.body:
So, what can you actually build by vibe coding? The short answer: a little bit of everything. The past year has felt like an explosion of AI-generated creativity across the software spectrum. Here are some of the domains where I’ve seen vibe coding in action:

Websites and Web Apps: This is the classic use-case. People are spinning up websites by just describing the layout and functionality. A personal example: I guided an AI to build a simple portfolio site for a photographer friend. I literally typed out: “Create a modern single-page website for a photographer named Jane Doe. Include a gallery of her photos (thumbnails that open in a lightbox), an about section, and a contact form that sends messages to her email.” Within minutes, the AI (using a model via Replit’s Ghostwriter) generated a working HTML/CSS/JS site with all those pieces. We tweaked the design by saying things like “Make the gallery grid 4 columns instead of 3” and “Add a dark mode toggle.” It was mind-blowing – a task that would normally require a web developer proficient in multiple technologies, accomplished through conversation. On a larger scale, startup founders are vibe-coding full-stack web apps. For example, I saw a demo of an AI-built task management SaaS (complete with user accounts, project boards, and a backend API) created by one person over a weekend. They described the features to an AI which produced the front-end code, backend server code, database schema, and even some basic unit tests. It wasn’t the prettiest code under the hood, but it worked.

slides.headline: Mobile Apps: With the help of AI, even mobile development is getting the vibe treatment.
slides.body: Mobile Apps: With the help of AI, even mobile development is getting the vibe treatment. Platforms like Bolt.new specifically allow you to prompt for a mobile app and get working code (for example, a React Native or Expo app) that you can immediately run. I played around with Bolt, typing “Build a simple mindfulness meditation app with a timer and calming background music” . The AI generated a cross-platform app with a start/pause timer and embedded audio, in one go. Of course, I had to supply the music file and fine-tune some UI text, but essentially I described an app and it was built . There are countless examples of developers using these tools to prototype app ideas: a weather app , a food diary , you name it. Some of these apps end up in app stores after a bit of polishing. It’s early days, but I can imagine a near future where entrepreneurs vibe code their app idea’s first version to test the market.

slides.headline: Games: Gamedev requires handling graphics, physics, input, etc., but even here vibe
slides.body: Games: Gamedev requires handling graphics, physics, input, etc., but even here vibe coding is making an impact. Indie game creators are using AI to generate chunks of Unity or Unreal Engine scripts by describing gameplay mechanics. I encountered a small YouTube community where folks do “AI game jams” – they challenge each other to build a playable game level purely through prompting. The results are simple 2D games or basic 3D scenes, but it’s impressive nonetheless. One example that stood out: a developer created a Flappy Bird clone by prompting ChatGPT (with Code Interpreter enabled) step by step – “make the bird jump on spacebar”, “add scoring when passing obstacles”, “add a game over screen”, etc. It required iterative prompting and debugging, but the entire codebase was essentially AI-written. In my own experiment, I asked an AI to “create a text adventure where the player explores a haunted mansion,” and got a surprisingly coherent Python game out of it. For more visual games, people often pair AI coding with AI-generated assets (images, sprites, textures from tools like DALL-E or Stable Diffusion). So not only the code, but also the artwork and music can now be synthesized. It’s vibe coding meets generative art – and it’s enabling solo creators to attempt projects that used to require whole teams.

slides.headline: VR/AR Experiences: As a VR enthusiast, this is one of my favorite areas being unlocked.
slides.body: VR/AR Experiences: As a VR enthusiast, this is one of my favorite areas being unlocked. I attended an XR developers meetup in San Francisco where, incredibly, someone live-demonstrated building a simple VR scene using vibe coding. They used a specialized AI-powered editor (the Windsurf editor, which is like a next-gen IDE from Codeium) and Cursor for code generation. In front of the crowd, they spoke out a description: “Create a virtual room with a wooden table in the center, put a 3D model of a cat on the table, and make the cat wave when I click on it.” Over the next few minutes, the AI produced the necessary code (in this case, using a webXR framework) and assets. We watched in real-time as the scene compiled and ran: sure enough, there was a virtual cat on a table in VR, and it waved its paw when triggered​ at AWE. The audience of devs was stunned – not because the scene was complex (it was a simple demo), but because of how effortlessly it came together. This approach, dubbed “ vibe coding for XR ,” is starting to catch on. AR developers can similarly ask for an AR effect or app by describing it (e.g. “place a floating info panel above recognized real-world objects”), and let the AI handle the heavy lifting of coding the interactions. It’s dramatically shortening the prototype cycle for XR; what used to take days in Unity could now take hours with an AI assistant. As someone who dabbles in AR, I’m personally excited that vibe coding is democratizing immersive experiences development – hopefully we’ll see an uptick in creative indie VR/AR projects thanks to this tech.

slides.headline: Full-Stack Software & Beyond: Perhaps the most ambitious use of vibe coding is to build
slides.body: Full-Stack Software & Beyond: Perhaps the most ambitious use of vibe coding is to build entire full-stack systems – not just a front-end or a script, but an application with front-end, back-end, database, and deployment. I won’t lie: doing this well is still very challenging for current AI tools, but people are attempting it. There’s a burgeoning concept of “AI as your software architect” where you describe a high-level solution and the AI generates multiple components. For instance, I worked with a small team where we tried to vibe-code an internal tool: a simple inventory tracking system. We told the AI (GPT-4 in this case) to create a backend service (we specified Python + FastAPI), a PostgreSQL database schema, and a web frontend (Vue.js) for it. The AI produced a surprising amount of boilerplate for all parts – database models, API endpoints, UI pages – in one go. We had to glue things together and fix mismatches (the API and UI didn’t perfectly align at first), but I’d estimate 70% of the code was generated by AI. Within a day, we had a basic full-stack app running. Granted, it was rough around the edges, but it proved a point: LLMs can play the role of multiple developers collaborating . In effect, the AI served as front-end developer, back-end developer, and devops (it even gave us a Dockerfile to deploy!). I’ve heard similar stories from others: one engineer had an AI write a cloud function and also set up the CI/CD pipeline config for it because he simply asked for it. This all hints at AI evolving into a full-stack collaborator , not just a code monkey for one layer.

slides.headline: The AI Toolbox: Models and Platforms Enabling Vibe Coding
slides.body:
None of this would be possible without the incredible AI models and tools under the hood. Let’s talk about the tech that makes vibe coding tick – basically, our AI coding toolbox .

Large Language Models (LLMs) for Code: At the heart of vibe coding are powerful LLMs that understand natural language and can generate code. When I’m “vibe coding,” I’m usually interfacing with one of these models:

OpenAI GPT-4: The trailblazer for many of us. GPT-4 (and its ChatGPT interface) is astonishingly good at not just writing code, but reasoning about what code should do from a description. I often use GPT-4 in a conversational way: “I need a function to sort a list of orders by date, can you write that in JavaScript?” – and poof, it appears. But more than that, GPT-4 will explain its code, fix mistakes when I point them out, and even suggest improvements if I ask. In vibe coding sessions, GPT-4 feels like a genius-level pair programmer who also happens to speak perfect English. Many early vibe coders cut their teeth using ChatGPT’s Code Interpreter mode or the API to generate whole modules of software. GPT-4 set the gold standard, and much of the vibe coding movement traces back to people experimenting with ChatGPT in late 2023 and realizing “Whoa, it can build X if I just describe X.”

slides.headline: Anthropic Claude: Another big player is Claude, especially the versions tuned for coding.
slides.body: Anthropic Claude: Another big player is Claude, especially the versions tuned for coding. Anthropic’s Claude model (particularly the Claude “Sonnet” series that emerged in 2024) became a favorite among developers for its code prowess. I’ve used Claude 2 and Claude “3.5-Sonnet” in a code editor setting; it tends to generate very clean code and handles larger context windows than GPT-4. This means I can feed it bigger codebases or lengthy project specs. In vibe coding, context is king – you might have the AI consider a multi-file project structure. Claude excels there. In fact, Karpathy’s own vibe coding tale involved Cursor with Sonnet , meaning he was leveraging Claude under the hood. Claude also often feels a bit more docile – it waits for guidance and won’t go off on tangents as easily. Some devs prefer its style, saying it’s like an obedient senior engineer that writes code methodically.

slides.headline: Google Gemini (and PaLM Code): As we moved into 2025, Google’s AI efforts ramped up.
slides.body: Google Gemini (and PaLM Code): As we moved into 2025, Google’s AI efforts ramped up. They introduced Gemini , a next-gen model, rumored to be highly capable at coding tasks. By the time of this writing, Google has been previewing “Gemini Pro” as an API that can rival GPT-4​. I haven’t gotten to play much with Gemini yet (it’s still in limited release), but I’ve seen some early testers show it building Android app code from prompts and even optimizing algorithms. Google also has specialized models like PaLM-Coder or Codey which power their internal tools (like the code assistant in Google Colab). It’s safe to say Google’s models will become part of the vibe coder’s toolkit once fully available. Imagine vibe coding an Android app via Google’s Android Studio assistant – that day is not far. Competition in the LLM space is heating up, and that’s great news for us creators.

slides.headline: Meta’s Code Llama and Open-Source Models: One exciting aspect is that you don’t strictly
slides.body: Meta’s Code Llama and Open-Source Models: One exciting aspect is that you don’t strictly need a proprietary service; open-source LLMs have been catching up. Meta released Code Llama in late 2023, a version of their LLaMA model tuned for programming. I’ve run Code Llama on my own PC to test local vibe coding. It’s not as powerful as GPT-4, but for simpler tasks it’s surprisingly competent. There’s something liberating about the idea that these capabilities could run offline or self-hosted – no need to send your code to a third-party cloud. The open-source community has built numerous coding models (StarCoder, GPT-NeoX variants, etc.), and while they might require more prompt effort, they open vibe coding to a wider audience and use cases (including privacy-sensitive projects). I know a data science team that uses a fine-tuned local model to generate Python data analysis scripts from plain English requests – effectively vibe coding their analytics, entirely behind their firewall. So, the ecosystem of models is diverse and growing more so.

slides.headline: Vibe-Friendly Development Platforms: Alongside the raw models, we have a crop of
slides.body:
Vibe-Friendly Development Platforms: Alongside the raw models, we have a crop of specialized tools and environments that make the vibe coding experience smoother. These are worth calling out:

Cursor: If vibe coding has an IDE of choice, Cursor might be it. Cursor is an AI-native code editor that gained notoriety after Karpathy praised it. I’ve been using Cursor for some projects – it basically looks like a regular coding environment, but you have an AI chat sidebar deeply integrated with your code. You can highlight a block of code and say, “Hey, what does this do?” or “Refactor this to use hooks instead of classes,” and it’ll do it. More importantly for vibe coding, you can describe high-level changes (like UI tweaks or new features) and Cursor’s AI will attempt to implement them across your codebase. It also has a voice input (through something called “SuperWhisper”), which means you can literally talk to it while your hands stay off the keyboard. That voice interaction is a trip – it feels like pair programming with an invisible partner. Cursor uses whatever model you hook it up to (GPT-4, Claude, etc.), acting as the friendly UI and context manager. Many vibe coders use Cursor to stay “in flow,” because you’re never leaving your editor to ask the AI for something – it’s all in one place, conversational and code-aware.

slides.headline: Replit Ghostwriter: Replit is a popular online coding platform, and their Ghostwriter AI
slides.body: Replit Ghostwriter: Replit is a popular online coding platform, and their Ghostwriter AI is like vibe coding on the web. Replit’s approach is making AI-assisted development accessible through just a browser – no heavy IDE needed. I’ve tried Ghostwriter on small Python and JavaScript projects: you start typing, and it autocompletes whole functions (like GitHub Copilot does), but you can also open a chat with it to ask for bigger tasks. For instance, I typed # TODO: implement user login in code, and then in Ghostwriter’s chat I wrote “Implement the user login function using JWT,” and it generated the function for me, integrated with my codebase. What’s neat is Replit allows real-time collaboration , so theoretically a human and an AI (Ghostwriter) and maybe another human can all be coding simultaneously in the same project. It blurs the lines between human and AI contributions. Replit has a huge community of young coders and learners, so vibe coding techniques are spreading there quickly. I sometimes browse Replit forums and see beginners sharing AI-generated snippets proudly, essentially saying “look what the AI helped me build!”

slides.headline: Vercel’s v0: V0.dev (pronounced “Vee-Zero”) is an experimental platform from Vercel that
slides.body: Vercel’s v0: V0.dev (pronounced “Vee-Zero”) is an experimental platform from Vercel that focuses on building web UIs and front-ends through natural language. I gave v0 a whirl and was impressed: you describe a webpage or component, and it produces the corresponding React/Vue code and a live preview. It’s almost like a design tool where the “design input” is your words. For example, I typed: “Create a navbar with a logo on the left and three links on the right (Home, About, Contact). Make the navbar sticky and add a drop shadow.” V0 generated a React component with TailwindCSS that matched the description, and I could see the preview instantly. The cool part was I could then drag and adjust the elements in the preview, and the underlying code would update – a blend of visual and language-based editing. V0’s strength is front-end prototyping; some developers use it to get the UI in place, then switch to another tool or manual coding for the backend. It’s very much aligned with vibe coding’s ethos: fast iteration from idea to interface . I recall reading a guide that recommended “have V0 make the UI layout first, then import into your IDE of choice”​. That’s a workflow I can relate to – let the AI handle the pixel pushing and boilerplate, then you focus on the business logic.

slides.headline: Lovable AI: One of the hottest new tools is Lovable (accessible at lovable.dev).
slides.body: Lovable AI: One of the hottest new tools is Lovable (accessible at lovable.dev). The tagline is essentially “build software 20× faster without writing code.” I’ve been playing with Lovable and it’s almost scary how far it goes. It presents a simple prompt box: “What do you want to build?” You then describe your app idea in a paragraph or two – the more detail, the better. I tested it with: “I need a web app for a personal cookbook. Users can add recipes with ingredients and instructions, upload a photo, and search through their recipes by ingredient or title. Include user accounts so my family can login and share recipes.” I hit enter, half-expecting an error or something generic. Instead, Lovable generated a multi-file project: a backend (Node.js) with API endpoints for recipes and user auth, a front-end (React) with pages for recipe listing, viewing, and adding, and even a simple database schema for MongoDB. It packaged this as a downloadable project. I was floored. The code was relatively boilerplate-y (not something a senior engineer would hand-craft), but it was functionally all there . Essentially a complete MVP of my cookbook idea in one go. Lovable is gaining traction especially among non-developers who have ideas but lack coding skills – it tries to make app creation as straightforward as writing a spec. There’s a lively discussion around it: some devs are worried tools like Lovable will “steal our jobs” (its marketing literally brags about doing what teams of developers do), while others see it as just another form of no-code. Either way, it’s an impressive showcase of what an AI can build from just a written concept​.

slides.headline: Bolt (by StackBlitz): Bolt.new is another rising star in the vibe coding toolkit,
slides.body: Bolt (by StackBlitz): Bolt.new is another rising star in the vibe coding toolkit, particularly for full-stack web apps. It’s actually built by the team behind StackBlitz (a well-known online IDE), but Bolt is more “agentic” – meaning it doesn’t just provide static suggestions; it actively executes tasks for you. I used Bolt to create a simple event listing web app. The experience was like having an all-in-one development agent: I told Bolt what I wanted, and it generated code for the front-end and back-end, set up a SQLite database, and even spun up a dev server to show me the result. Bolt has a neat trick where it can integrate with external services – for example, I could say, “Also, add Stripe payments for premium events” and since Bolt has some Stripe integration, it scaffolded code to connect to Stripe’s API. It can deploy apps too: after the app was working locally, I clicked “Deploy” and Bolt pushed it to a cloud hosting (with a URL ready to share). This blew my mind: from idea to live app, all within Bolt, using mostly natural language and a few button clicks. It’s the closest I’ve felt to having an “AI engineer” that not only codes but also runs and deploys the project. No wonder Bolt and similar tools have been magnets for VC funding – they’re shaping up to be the next major productivity platforms for developers​.

slides.headline: Windsurf (by Codeium): I mentioned Windsurf earlier in the VR example.
slides.body: Windsurf (by Codeium): I mentioned Windsurf earlier in the VR example. Windsurf is essentially Codeium’s AI-powered IDE that’s built for vibe coding workflows. What sets it apart is its emphasis on a seamless feedback loop: you can see your app live in a preview pane, interact with it, and then tell the AI to change things you see. For instance, in Windsurf I loaded a web app preview and literally clicked on a button in the preview and said, “Make this button red and increase its padding,” and the AI identified the corresponding code and changed the CSS accordingly. It’s almost uncanny – like the tool reads your mind through your clicks. Windsurf also supports multi-file context, running commands, and deploying straight from the IDE​. Codeium’s aim is clearly to make the entire development cycle AI-assisted: write code, run it, test it, debug it, deploy it, all with an AI copilot deeply integrated. I’ve found Windsurf particularly useful for debugging vibe-coded projects: when something breaks, you can hit a button to “send error to AI” and it analyzes the error log or stack trace and suggests a fix​. It’s like pair programming with a built-in debugger that actually knows your codebase. I suspect we’ll see more of this “see it, shape it, ship it” style in future IDEs – because it lowers the friction between having an idea, testing it live, and getting it out to users.

slides.headline: And beyond these, there are many other tools and plugins: from Visual Studio Code’s
slides.body: And beyond these, there are many other tools and plugins: from Visual Studio Code’s Copilot Chat extension to JetBrains AI Assistant , to niche ones like Fig AI for terminal commands. The landscape is rich and evolving. The unifying theme is that AI is being woven into every developer tool , enabling this vibe-led workflow. Where we used to write code, now we increasingly describe and direct .

slides.headline: When AI Joins Your Team: Developers’ Evolving Role
slides.body:
As someone who’s been writing code for over a decade, adopting vibe coding has been both exhilarating and humbling. Exhilarating because I can build faster than ever; humbling because it’s changed the way I think about my own role in the process. Let’s talk about how the role of developers (and creators in general) is evolving in this new paradigm.

From Code Author to Code Curator: Traditionally, a developer’s job is to write code – to be the author crafting each line. In vibe coding, the AI does a lot of that authorship. I’ve felt my own focus shift from writing to guiding and curating . Now, I spend more time deciding what to build and reviewing what the AI wrote , rather than typing it out myself. It’s as if I’ve become an editor and architect, and the AI is the one banging out the first draft. This requires a different mindset: I frame problems for the AI in clear language (prompt engineering is a skill!), and when it responds with code, I inspect that code not line-by-line as I would if I wrote it, but at a higher level. I ask, “Does this do roughly what we need? Are there obvious errors or risky bits?” If it’s mostly right, I accept it and move on. If not, I give feedback to the AI: “This isn’t handling the edge case of X, please fix that,” or sometimes I’ll say “Scrap this approach and try a different technique.” In a way, I’m like a project manager assigning tasks to a very smart but occasionally wayward developer (the AI). I’ve had to let go of the ego of being the one who personally codes every solution. Instead, I take pride in orchestrating a good solution via the AI. It’s a different kind of satisfaction when something works and you know you collaborated with an AI to get there.

slides.headline: The Rise of Prompt Engineering: Writing good prompts has become an art.
slides.body: The Rise of Prompt Engineering: Writing good prompts has become an art. The difference between a mediocre AI output and an excellent one often comes down to how you ask. I’ve learned to be explicit in my instructions to AI: specify the tech stack I want, give examples of input/output if possible, and even mention constraints (“make sure to handle up to 1000 concurrent users” or “the code should follow our style conventions”). Sometimes I even write prompts that mimic a spec document. For example, instead of “make a chat feature,” I’ll say: “Implement a chat feature with these requirements: 1) Real-time updates using websockets, 2) Store chat history in database, 3) Include timestamps, 4) Provide a ‘typing…’ indicator.” The difference is night and day – the AI’s output for a detailed prompt like that is far closer to what I want, often with minimal corrections needed. It feels very much like writing a thorough ticket for a teammate. We joke that the hottest new programming language is English , and there’s truth to that: clear written communication is becoming a core developer skill. I’ve even seen job postings looking for “AI developer” or “prompt engineer” roles where one key responsibility is crafting prompts and workflows for AI coding systems. It’s a bit surreal, but also logical – in vibe coding, knowing how to talk to the machine is as important as knowing how to talk to other humans in a team.

slides.headline: Quality Assurance and Testing Are Critical: A big chunk of a developer’s evolving role is
slides.body: Quality Assurance and Testing Are Critical: A big chunk of a developer’s evolving role is being the quality filter. If you let the AI code freely without oversight, things can go off the rails. I’ve had AI-written code that looked perfectly confident but contained subtle bugs or security issues. For example, an AI might introduce a SQL query that’s vulnerable to injection if not careful, or it might use an inefficient approach that doesn’t scale. Part of my new job is to review and test the AI’s output thoroughly. I always remind myself (and any juniors experimenting with vibe coding): trust, but verify . These AIs can produce incorrect or nonsensical code with the same smiling confidence as correct code. So you need a human in the loop who understands the problem domain enough to catch mistakes. Personally, I write more unit tests now, and sometimes I even ask the AI to generate those tests (it will happily produce tests for the code it wrote, which is interesting). When an AI-generated function passes a robust test suite I crafted, I start to feel more at ease. In vibe coding teams, I foresee a possible shift where some members focus primarily on writing tests and validation scripts, effectively “guarding” the quality while others focus on prompting the AI to add features. The dynamic is like one person rapidly building, another person rigorously testing – except the builder is half-automated.

slides.headline: Debugging by Conversation: Debugging has changed too.
slides.body: Debugging by Conversation: Debugging has changed too. In the past, I’d stare at a stack trace, dig through code, maybe add some print statements. Now, when something breaks, my instinct is: ask the AI . I copy the error message and say, “The app crashed with this error. What might be the cause?” Nine times out of ten, the AI points me in the right direction or fixes it outright. It’s like having a debugger that can analyze the problem with you. However, if the AI itself caused the bug by writing flawed code, it sometimes struggles to fix what it doesn’t fully understand. In those cases, I have to step in with my own knowledge. One weird thing I’ve noticed: vibe coding forces you to maintain some level of understanding of the codebase, even if you didn’t write it all. Because if something’s really off, you’re the final authority to diagnose it. I had a bug the AI couldn’t solve – it kept applying band aid fixes that didn’t address the root cause. I ended up reading through the code (a chunk of AI-generated logic for caching results) and discovered a fundamental flaw. I then explained to the AI what the flaw was, and only then could it properly fix it. This taught me that while vibe coding can spare you from writing a lot of code, it doesn’t spare you from thinking deeply about that code’s behavior. In fact, you may need to think more in order to guide an AI which doesn’t truly understand the problem the way you do. So yes, I debug differently now – often via dialogue – but I also keep my classical debugging skills sharp for those times when I need to outthink the machine.

slides.headline: Architect, Designer, Visionary: Perhaps the most gratifying change is that I get to focus
slides.body: Architect, Designer, Visionary: Perhaps the most gratifying change is that I get to focus more on the creative and high-level aspects of software. Since I spend less energy on rote coding, I can allocate more brainpower to the app’s design, the user experience, and new ideas. It reminds me of moving from being an individual contributor to a tech lead – you zoom out from the nitty-gritty and look at the whole system. Vibe coding allows even a solo dev to take that higher-level view. For instance, while AI churns out yet another CRUD form, I might sketch how the overall user flow should work, or consider the data model implications of a new feature. I think about edge cases and how to prompt the AI to handle them. In a sense, developers are becoming more like product designers and problem solvers , and the AI is the one translating those solutions into code. I find that enjoyable. It’s the fun part of software development – solving puzzles and imagining features – without as much of the slog of implementation. Of course, many developers (myself included) enjoy programming for its own sake, and vibe coding can feel like it’s stealing the joy of coding. I admit I sometimes miss writing a beautifully optimized algorithm by hand. So I’ll do it manually to scratch that itch. But for a lot of everyday programming tasks, I don’t mind offloading them to AI. It frees up time to be creative and pursue more projects than I could before. Some of my peers have started calling themselves “software directors” – like a film director guiding a crew, we guide the AI crew to produce the software vision we have. It’s a cheesy analogy, but it does feel that way at times.

slides.headline: Collaboration and Communication: The human role also shifts in collaborative settings.
slides.body: Collaboration and Communication: The human role also shifts in collaborative settings. If two or more developers are working with AI assistants on a project, communication is key. We have to sync not just with each other, but also ensure we’re instructing our respective AIs in a compatible way. I encountered a scenario where a teammate and I were both vibe coding different modules of an app. My AI was producing code with a certain style and assumptions, and his AI had a slightly different approach. When we merged, things didn’t fit well initially (different database schemas, etc.). We realized we needed to agree on some design choices upfront and then feed those agreements into our AI prompts so that both AIs work toward the same vision. This is new – essentially, we had to do a bit of “prompt documentation” for consistency. Additionally, when he had the AI write a chunk of code, I would review it, and vice versa, much like code review but with the awareness that an AI wrote it. Sometimes I’d ask, “Did you prompt it to consider security for this part?” and if not, we’d re-prompt to harden the code. So human-to-human collaboration now includes discussing how we use the AI, not just the end code. It adds an interesting layer to teamwork, and I think as teams formalize this, we’ll see methodologies or best practices emerge (maybe an agile process where some tickets are explicitly marked for AI execution, etc.).

slides.headline: At the end of the day, I feel developers aren’t so much being replaced as they are
slides.body: At the end of the day, I feel developers aren’t so much being replaced as they are evolving . The role is shifting from craftsman to conductor . You still need to deeply understand software engineering principles – arguably even more so, to catch AI’s mistakes – but you apply that knowledge differently. It’s less about hand-coding every line, more about making high-level decisions, coordinating AI efforts, and ensuring the final product meets requirements. For me, it’s been a journey of learning to let go when appropriate and step in when necessary, and always keep learning (because these tools change fast!).

slides.headline: The Buzz in Tech Circles: Hype, Skepticism, and the Future of Coding
slides.body:
No conversation about vibe coding is complete without addressing what everyone in the tech world seems to be asking: Is this the real deal, or just another buzzword? Depending on who you talk to, vibe coding is either the dawn of a new era or just a fancy term for AI-assisted programming with a marketing spin. As someone immersed in this space, I’ve heard it all.

The Hype – “This Changes Everything”: There’s a palpable excitement among many of us that vibe coding hints at the future of how software will be built. Tech influencers on Twitter are calling vibe coding “the next evolution of coding” . Some venture capitalists are even saying things like “If you’re not vibe coding, you’ll be left behind,” echoing what Y Combinator’s CEO Garry Tan said in that discussion​. The optimistic viewpoint is that AI will democratize coding , finally making the longstanding dream of “everyone can code” a reality – except without everyone actually needing to learn code. Just as the move from assembly to high-level languages made programming more accessible, the move from traditional coding to natural language “vibing” could open the floodgates for millions more creators. I’ve had non-engineer colleagues build small tools for themselves using vibe coding, and they were giddy with the empowerment it gave them. That’s a big deal: people solving their own problems with software, without a developer as the middleman. In tech meetups, I often hear references to earlier shifts like the introduction of visual programming or no-code tools , and how this goes beyond, because the AI can handle complexity not possible in simple no-code platforms. True believers see vibe coding as not just a productivity boost for coders, but as a creative renaissance – where the limiting factor becomes one’s imagination, not technical chops. There’s also excitement that this could lead to a boom in software innovation: if prototyping an app or feature is now 10× faster, we can try ten times more ideas, leading to more breakthroughs and niche solutions. The vibe coding community online frequently shares success stories – “I built X in a day, which would have taken me weeks before!” – and it fuels this sense that we’re on the cusp of something revolutionary.

slides.headline: The Skepticism – “Hold On, It’s Not Magic”: On the flip side, many veteran developers and
slides.body:
The Skepticism – “Hold On, It’s Not Magic”: On the flip side, many veteran developers and industry observers urge caution. I was chatting with an experienced engineer friend who quipped, “Vibe coding? More like vibe hacking. It’s fine for toy projects, but would you trust it for a pacemaker’s software or a banking system? No way.” This sentiment is echoed by experts like Gary Marcus (a prominent AI critic) who called out that some vibe-coded apps are basically just regurgitating existing code and ideas, not truly innovating​. The concerns break down into a few key points:

First, code quality and maintainability . AI-generated code can be messy under the hood. It might work initially but be a nightmare to maintain. Imagine inheriting a large codebase that was vibe-coded – with the original “developer” not really knowing why the AI wrote things a certain way. Professional devs worry about technical debt: are we trading short-term speed for long-term pain? A common refrain: If you didn’t write it, you may struggle to debug or extend it. I’ve felt this myself when revisiting an AI-written module months later; I had to re-learn what it was doing, almost as if I was reading someone else’s code (because I was – the “someone else” just happened to be an AI).

slides.headline: Second, reliability and correctness .
slides.body:
Second, reliability and correctness . We know AI can make mistakes, sometimes dumb ones, sometimes subtle ones. In a production system, those mistakes could be costly. A security bug introduced by an AI could open a hole for hackers. As one developer advocate put it, “You can’t just let the robots run wild without checking their work, or you’ll get yourself into trouble” ​. Many in the field stress that vibe coding needs a solid safety net: code reviews, tests, oversight by someone with technical expertise. The Guardian wrote an article basically saying “you don’t need code to be a programmer now, but you still need expertise”​​ – that captures it well.

Third, the knowledge gap for newbies . While vibe coding lowers the entry barrier, some argue it might give a false sense of competence. A beginner might string together an app via AI, but if they never learn why the code works, they could be in trouble when things go off-script. I’ve seen this firsthand: a friend with minimal coding background built a working web app with AI, but when it started crashing due to a subtle bug, he was totally lost. If the AI couldn’t fix it, he had no idea what to do. It’s like someone who learned to drive with an AI co-pilot always holding the wheel – when the co-pilot steps away, can they handle the road alone? Some experienced devs see this as dangerous: junior engineers might skip learning fundamentals, which are still needed to truly ensure software is robust. An AI advocate might respond that maybe the AI co-pilot will never step away. But in any non-trivial project, it eventually will hit a limit or error where human insight is needed. As AI researcher Simon Willison nicely put it: if you carefully review and understand all the AI’s code, then you’re just using AI as an assistant, not vibe coding per say – implying that true vibe coding (where you don’t understand all the code) is something to be very wary of, especially for production systems.

slides.headline: Fourth, ethics and originality .
slides.body: Fourth, ethics and originality . There’s a debate about whether AI-generated code is truly “new” or just remixing training data. Karpathy and others have noted that as long as it works, maybe it doesn’t matter how it was made​. But some critics like Gary Marcus (again) point out that being impressed by an AI spitting out a known solution isn’t the same as human creativity or understanding​. There’s also the matter of attribution – if an AI regurgitated code that was in its training set (say, a well-known open-source library function), are vibe coders unknowingly plagiarizing? The legal and licensing questions around AI-generated code are still unresolved. Companies are treading carefully; I know of at least one big tech firm that restricts using AI for code unless the model is known to be trained on proper licensed data, because they fear a lawsuit down the line claiming IP infringement. So while vibe coding is fun and productive, the professionalization of it will require navigating these issues.

slides.headline: In tech circles, this mix of hype and skepticism often leads to lively (sometimes heated)
slides.body: In tech circles, this mix of hype and skepticism often leads to lively (sometimes heated) discussions. I’ve sat in on engineering meetings where half the team was excited to incorporate more AI, and the other half was pushing back hard, raising all the aforementioned concerns. One senior architect said something like, “Just because Karpathy can vibe out a weekend project doesn’t mean our team can ship mission-critical code that way.” That’s a fair point. The consensus that seems to be emerging is that vibe coding is excellent for prototyping, exploration, and personal projects , and it’s gradually finding its place in production workflows with proper checks. But full-on vibe coding (as originally defined, where you don’t even look at the code) is not widely adopted for serious, large-scale software yet – nor should it be, until the tools and practices mature.

slides.headline: Signals for the Future: Where is this all heading?
slides.body:
Signals for the Future: Where is this all heading? I often ask myself that as I alternate between marveling at what I can do now and cringing at the rough edges that still exist.

In a way, vibe coding feels like a glimpse of what coding might look like in 5 or 10 years. Today, it’s at the cutting edge – early adopters and enthusiasts are showing it off, some companies are dipping their toes. If the trend continues, tomorrow it might become mainstream. I envision a future IDE (maybe a successor to VS Code or something entirely new) where the default mode is conversational. Instead of opening a new file and typing, you’d create a new module by saying, “Hey AI, I need a module for managing user profiles with these fields… go ahead and set that up.” The AI does the boilerplate, then you refine. Writing code by hand might become a niche activity, reserved for special low-level optimizations or pleasure, much like writing assembly is today.

slides.headline: It also signals that the abstraction level of programming is rising .
slides.body: It also signals that the abstraction level of programming is rising . We went from machine code to assembly to high-level languages, and now to natural language. Each jump made programming more accessible and powerful, though it also abstracted away some control. Vibe coding is the next jump – code at the level of ideas and intent. This could unlock programming to millions who were shut out before. I find that inspiring: imagine artists, scientists, doctors, anyone with domain knowledge but not coding skills, being able to create software to solve their problems by just explaining what they need. We see hints of this already – an ecologist friend of mine described an analysis tool they wanted and basically vibe-coded a rough version with GPT, something they’d been asking their IT department to help with for ages.

slides.headline: Another future angle is the convergence of AI agents .
slides.body: Another future angle is the convergence of AI agents . Right now, vibe coding typically involves one AI assisting one developer. But there are projects experimenting with multiple AI “agents” that can coordinate – one might generate code, another might generate tests for that code, another might check for security issues, all orchestrated by a master agent. This multi-agent approach could result in a sort of autonomous coding assembly line (there was buzz about systems like “AutoGPT” that attempt autonomy). It’s not mature yet – often these agents get confused or stuck in loops – but it hints at future tools where you spin up an entire virtual software team: “Architect AI, give me a design; Coder AI, implement it; Tester AI, verify it; DevOps AI, deploy it.” As a human, you’d oversee the collaboration and step in when needed. It sounds wild, but not unimaginable given current trajectories.

slides.headline: Crucially, I think the human role will remain vital.
slides.body:
Crucially, I think the human role will remain vital. The nature of it will change, as we discussed. If vibe coding truly becomes dominant, being a great software creator might be less about knowing every syntax quirk and more about having strong problem-solving skills, domain understanding, and an intuition for guiding AI effectively. It might also require more soft skills – communication, coordinating between stakeholders and AI, etc. Perhaps coding will be seen less as an engineering discipline and more as a design/communication discipline. That’s a big shift.

In tech circles, there’s also talk about how this affects jobs and the industry. Will we need fewer programmers? Or will we simply tackle bigger challenges with the same number of people? Historically, when tools get better, ambition grows. We don’t see companies laying off all frontend devs because we got React or laying off all ops engineers because we got cloud automation – instead, we build more complex systems. Similarly, vibe coding might not shrink the software workforce; it could just mean we aim higher, build software we couldn’t before, or address bespoke needs that weren’t worth the cost previously. That said, the skill profile may change. Junior devs might need to adapt quickly – the duties of an “entry-level coder” in 2030 could be very different from today. Universities and bootcamps are already scrambling to include AI coding in curricula, which is telling.

slides.headline: Finally, vibe coding’s rise is stirring philosophical questions: If the act of coding
slides.body: Finally, vibe coding’s rise is stirring philosophical questions: If the act of coding becomes as simple as telling a story, does the meaning of “being a programmer” change? Many programmers (myself included) identify with the craft of coding. It’s creative and logical and has a certain flow state. If that grunt work diminishes, some worry the job might become less satisfying – “all the fun parts will be done by AI, and I’m just left babysitting it.” I empathize with this sentiment, but I also find that new joys emerge. There’s a certain magic in collaborating with an AI – when it surprises you with a clever solution or saves you hours, it’s delightful. And you can always dip back into hands-on coding when you want; vibe coding doesn’t forbid that. In the end, I suspect coding will bifurcate: routine programming might largely be automated, while high-stakes or highly creative programming will remain a human art (with AI as a tool). This could elevate the overall level of innovation, as developers channel their energy into the really hard or novel problems.

slides.headline: As I wrap up this deep dive, I’ll share a personal reflection: Vibe coding has rekindled
slides.body:
As I wrap up this deep dive, I’ll share a personal reflection: Vibe coding has rekindled some childlike wonder in me. I feel like I’m in a sci-fi novel, commanding a computer with my voice and it just does things. It reminds me of when I first learned to code – that feeling of power and possibility, making the computer do whatever I could imagine (within BASIC’s limits, back then!). Now the limits are pushing out further than ever. We’re not quite at “computer, build me an MMO game” and boom it’s done – but we’re inching in that direction.

Will future generations even distinguish between “coding” and just “telling the computer what you need”? Possibly not. As one optimistic colleague declared, “The best programmer 10 years from now may well be someone who never writes a single line of code themselves.” It sounds paradoxical, but it could be true.

slides.headline: For now, vibe coding is our fascinating present and likely our future.
slides.body: For now, vibe coding is our fascinating present and likely our future. It’s altering the fabric of software development in real time. And I, for one, am enjoying the ride – with one hand on the keyboard and the other firmly on the vibe.
